summary: Revises all Enumservices previously registered with IANA under the now obsolete rules of RFC 3761, bringing them in line with the newer registry procedure. It updates a number of earlier RFCs that defined those Enumservices. It is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: Cleaning old entries in a library catalog so they follow the new filing rules.

subtitle: Bringing legacy telephone number service registries up to current standards

tldr.problem: IANA had Enumservice registrations created under old RFC 3761 rules that did not conform to newer guidelines in RFC 6117. These legacy entries needed standardization.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC catalogs all 39 legacy Enumservices and converts each one to the new XML-chunk format with proper metadata elements, making them consistent with current registration procedures.
tldr.outcome: IANA now maintains a unified registry of Enumservices using the same structure and requirements for all entries, reducing confusion and inconsistency.

today: RFC 6118 updated all legacy Enumservice registrations to comply with RFC 6117. The IANA Enumservice registry now uses a uniform XML format for all 39 services.

sections.title: Why Legacy Registrations Needed Updating
sections.content:
RFC 3761 defined the ENUM system, which lets telephone numbers be resolved into web addresses through DNS. Services registered under RFC 3761 could be designated by phone numbers, and the system would return URIs pointing to the right protocol (like mailto:, sip:, tel:, or http:).

In 2011, RFC 6117 replaced RFC 3761 with stricter requirements for how these Enumservices must be registered. The new standard required XML chunks with specific metadata elements that the old registrations lacked. To maintain consistency across the entire IANA registry, all 39 legacy Enumservices had to be reformatted.

Importantly, this document does not change what the services do or how they work. It only updates the registration format and adds missing metadata so every entry follows the same rules.
sections.plainLanguage: When a filing system changes, old entries need their labels updated even if the documents inside the folders stay the same.

sections.title: What This RFC Does and Does Not Change
sections.content:
This RFC converts each of the 39 legacy Enumservice registrations to the new XML format. Each entry includes its functional specification (what the service is for), the URI schemes it can use, a class designation, security notes, and usage level.

The update adds required metadata fields that RFC 6117 now mandates: a class field that categorizes the service as either application-based or data type-based, and an explicit usage field showing whether the service is COMMON or a SUBSET of another.

What the RFC does not do is complete missing sections in the original Enumservice specifications themselves. Those RFCs still need their own updates to fully conform to RFC 6117.
sections.plainLanguage: The update adds the new filing labels required by the new rules, but does not rewrite the descriptions or change what the services do.

sections.title: The Registry, Enumservices, and URI Schemes
sections.content:
An Enumservice is a named service in the ENUM system that describes how a telephone number can connect to a particular communication method. Examples include voice:tel (voice calls via the tel: URI), sip (SIP calls), email:mailto (email), and web:https (web access over secure HTTP).

Each service is a combination of a type and a subtype. For instance, voice:tel has type voice and subtype tel. The urischeme specifies which URI protocols the service will return: a voice:tel service returns tel: URIs.

The IANA registry is the central list maintained by IANA that publishes all approved Enumservices. Each entry must now include elements like functional specification, class, usage level, and security considerations.
sections.plainLanguage: An Enumservice is like a postal sorting category: 'deliver voice calls', 'send emails', 'web access'. Each one lists what protocol it uses and what the rules are for it.

sections.title: The 39 Legacy Enumservices Converted
sections.content:
The RFC systematically covers 39 services. Major categories include:

  • Email and messaging: email:mailto, ems:mailto, ems:tel, sms:mailto, sms:tel, mms:mailto, mms:tel, voicemsg:*, videomsg:*, unifmsg:*
  • Voice and presence: voice:tel, h323, sip, pres (presence), xmpp, im (instant messaging)
  • Web and file transfer: web:http, web:https, ft:ftp, vcard (electronic business cards)
  • Legacy services: fax:tel, ifax:mailto, pstn:sip, pstn:tel, ical-access:http, ical-access:https, ical-sched:mailto, vpim:ldap, vpim:mailto

Each entry includes its functional specification (reused from the original RFC that registered it), the new class designation, and security guidance. Many services reference security sections in their originating RFCs rather than repeating the content.
sections.plainLanguage: The document lists 39 ways to reach someone or connect a phone number: by email, voice, video, instant message, web page, fax, and others. Each one gets the proper filing label.

sections.title: IESG Actions and Approval Process Changes
sections.content:
Under RFC 3761, any Enumservice registration had to be published in a Standards Track, Experimental, or Best Current Practice RFC. This meant every new service required a full RFC, which was a high bar.

RFC 6117 dropped this requirement. Now Specification Required is sufficient, which means a Designated Expert from IANA reviews the request and the specification. This allows faster registration of new services without the overhead of full RFC publication.

This RFC updates the IESG's approval policy to reflect the new process. The change makes the registry more agile while still maintaining quality control through expert review.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of needing a whole new book (RFC) to add a service to the filing system, the librarian now just needs to review the proposal and approve it.

sections.title: Security Impact
sections.content:
This RFC does not introduce any new technology or protocol, so there are no new security issues. Each Enumservice's security properties are inherited from the protocol it uses (SIP, email, HTTP, etc.).

The document preserves all security guidance from the original registrations. Each service's XML chunk includes a security element that either embeds security considerations or references the relevant section in the original RFC.

By standardizing the registration format, the update actually improves clarity about security properties: every service now has its security guidance explicitly documented in a consistent location.
sections.plainLanguage: This is just paperwork. The services themselves and how safe they are does not change.
